capital: Pretoria (administrative capital); Cape Town (legislative capital); Bloemfontein (judicial capital)
summary: South Africa lies at the southern tip of Africa, with three capitals and 12 official languages; after the apartheid system it held its first democratic elections in 1994 and is known as the "Rainbow Nation."

ranking.name: Christianity
ranking.description: In 1652 the Dutch East India Company established a supply station at the Cape, bringing the Dutch Reformed Church; after the British colonization of the 19th century, the London Missionary Society, the Methodists and the Anglicans preached widely among Africans, and mission schools such as Lovedale trained the first generation of African intellectuals. From the late 19th century Africans founded independent churches of their own, and the Zion Christian Church, founded in 1924, is now the largest church in South Africa. The Reformed Church provided theological justification for apartheid, while the Anglican Archbishop Tutu won the 1984 Nobel Peace Prize for opposing apartheid.

ranking.name: No religion
ranking.description: Those with no religion are concentrated mainly among young people in cities and the highly educated, related to urbanization, modern education and globalization. After the end of apartheid society became more open and diverse, and some people feel alienated from the church's historical association with apartheid. Overall, however, South Africa is still a highly religious society, and the share with no religion is not high.

ranking.name: Traditional beliefs
ranking.description: Traditional belief is centered on ancestor veneration, holding that ancestors protect or punish their descendants, and traditional healers, the "sangomas," communicate with the ancestors through divination and herbs. In practice most Black South African Christians also take part in ancestor veneration and traditional rituals, so the share identifying only with traditional belief is low, but its cultural influence is far broader than the figures show.

ranking.name: Islam
ranking.description: Islam was first brought in the 17th-18th centuries by slaves and political exiles that the Dutch East India Company brought from Indonesia and the Malay region; the Indonesian scholar Sheikh Yusuf, exiled in 1694, was an important figure, and in 1794 the first mosque was built in the Bo-Kaap district of Cape Town, forming the "Cape Malay" community. After 1860 Indian Muslim merchants and laborers who came to Natal also brought Islam, mainly concentrated in Cape Town and Durban.

ranking.name: Hinduism
ranking.description: From 1860 Britain recruited indentured laborers from India to work on the sugar plantations of Natal; most of them were Hindus, and Indian merchants moved in afterward. Durban thus became home to one of the largest Indian communities in Africa, and Mahatma Gandhi also worked in the campaign against discrimination in South Africa from 1893 to 1914. Hindus are still concentrated mainly in KwaZulu-Natal Province.

religion.background: South Africa's indigenous Khoisan and Bantu peoples originally worshipped ancestral spirits and nature spirits. Dutch colonization in 1652 brought the Reformed Church, and after British colonization in the 19th century various Protestant denominations preached on a large scale, while the Cape Malay community and Indian immigrants in Natal brought Islam and Hinduism. From the late 19th century Africans founded independent churches that blended Christianity with traditional beliefs. During the apartheid period the churches included both defenders of the system and resisters such as Tutu; after democratization in 1994 the constitution guaranteed freedom of religion.

language.official: South Africa has 12 official languages, including Zulu, Xhosa, Afrikaans, English and South African Sign Language.

ranking.name: Zulu
ranking.description: Zulu belongs to the Nguni branch of the Bantu family; in the early 19th century the Zulu king Shaka (reigned about 1816-1828) unified the tribes and expanded outward, making the Zulu Kingdom one of the most powerful forces in southern Africa. The Zulu live mainly in KwaZulu-Natal Province, and many have also moved to Gauteng Province, where Johannesburg is located, to work. In 1994 Zulu became one of the official languages, and it is the most widely spoken mother tongue in South Africa.

ranking.name: Xhosa
ranking.description: Xhosa is spoken in the Eastern Cape and has many click sounds borrowed from Khoisan languages. The Xhosa and the Cape Colony fought a century of frontier wars between 1779 and 1879, and they were also among the first peoples to receive missionary education; the Lovedale mission press published early Xhosa literature. Many anti-apartheid leaders, such as Mandela, were Xhosa.

ranking.name: Afrikaans
ranking.description: Afrikaans derives from the Dutch of the 17th-century Dutch colonists and gradually simplified and formed an independent language through contact with Malay slaves and the Khoikhoi in the Cape Colony; in 1925 it replaced Dutch as an official language. The apartheid government forced Black schools to teach in Afrikaans, which provoked the 1976 Soweto student uprising. Today its speakers include, besides the Afrikaners, the even more numerous Coloured community.

ranking.name: Northern Sotho (Sepedi)
ranking.description: Northern Sotho (Sepedi) is spoken mainly in Limpopo Province in the north. In the 19th century the Pedi Kingdom, led by King Sekhukhune, resisted Boer and British expansion before being defeated by British forces in 1879. During apartheid the Northern Sotho-speaking people were assigned to "homelands," and after 1994 Northern Sotho became one of the official languages.

ranking.name: English
ranking.description: Britain first occupied the Cape in 1795 and formally acquired rule in 1806, and in 1820 large numbers of British settlers arrived in the Eastern Cape. English thereafter became the language of the colonial government, commerce and mining; after democratization in 1994, English dominates government, the media and higher education as a neutral common language among ethnic groups, though fewer than one in ten speak it as a mother tongue.

ranking.name: Tswana
ranking.description: Tswana is spoken in the North West Province and is the same as the national language of neighboring Botswana. In 1857 the missionary Robert Moffat completed the translation of the Tswana Bible, the first complete Bible translated into an African language in southern Africa. During apartheid the government set up the nominally independent "Bophuthatswana" homeland, which was reintegrated into South Africa after 1994.

language.history: The earliest inhabitants of South Africa, the Khoisan, spoke Khoisan languages with click sounds, and when the Bantu peoples migrated south they brought languages such as Zulu, Xhosa and Sotho. Dutch colonization in 1652 brought Dutch, which later evolved into Afrikaans; after British rule in 1806 English became the colonial language. During apartheid only English and Afrikaans were official languages, and the forced teaching in Afrikaans in 1976 triggered the Soweto uprising. The 1994 democratic constitution recognized 11 official languages, and in 2023 South African Sign Language was added.

ranking.name: Braai
ranking.description: Fire is made in the open with wood or charcoal to grill various meats such as steak, lamb chops, boerewors and chicken, served with maize porridge, salads and spicy vegetable relish.
ranking.history: Charcoal grilling combines the food traditions of African cattle-herding peoples with those of Dutch and German immigrants and Boer pioneers since the 17th century, and the word "braai" comes from the Afrikaans for "to grill." In South Africa the braai is not only a way of cooking but a social activity that crosses race and class. From 2005 a popular campaign promoted calling Heritage Day on 24 September "National Braai Day," encouraging people of different groups to share food around the fire.

ranking.name: Bobotie
ranking.description: Minced meat seasoned with curry powder, spices, raisins and apricot jam is topped with a custard of egg and milk and baked; it tastes slightly sweet with a curry fragrance and is often served with yellow rice.
ranking.history: Bobotie is the representative dish of Cape Malay cuisine; in the 17th-18th centuries the Dutch East India Company brought slaves and exiles from Indonesia and the Malay region to the Cape, and they combined Southeast Asian spices and cooking techniques with the Dutch minced-meat dishes to create this dish. It reflects the history in which Indian Ocean trade and slavery were intertwined during South Africa's colonial period. Today bobotie is regarded by many as the national dish of South Africa and is often made for family gatherings and holidays.

ranking.name: Biltong
ranking.description: Beef or game such as antelope is cut into long strips, cured with salt, vinegar, coriander seed and black pepper and air-dried, making a dried meat that keeps for a long time.
ranking.history: Indigenous Africans had long dried meat, and from the 17th century Dutch colonists added vinegar and spices for curing, developing today's biltong. The name comes from the Dutch "bil" (rump) and "tong" (strip). When the Boers began the "Great Trek" into the interior in the 1830s, biltong was an indispensable food for their long journey. Today it is South Africans' favorite snack while watching rugby, and it has also traveled with emigrants to Britain and Australia.

ranking.name: Bunny chow
ranking.description: A whole or half loaf of bread is hollowed out and filled with piping-hot curried mutton, chicken or beans, and the scooped-out bread is used to dip in the curry.
ranking.history: Bunny chow was born in the mid-20th century in the Indian community of Durban and has nothing to do with rabbits. The name is generally believed to come from a corruption of "bania" (an Indian merchant caste). There are several accounts of its origin, one of which is that during apartheid Black laborers could not enter certain restaurants to eat, so Indian restaurants put curry in hollowed-out bread for them to take away. Today it is Durban's most representative street food, reflecting the history of South Africa's Indian community and apartheid.

ranking.name: Boerewors
ranking.description: A coarse-ground sausage of beef with pork or lamb, seasoned with coriander seed, cloves, nutmeg and vinegar, coiled in a spiral and grilled over charcoal.
ranking.history: Boerewors derives from the sausage-making tradition of Dutch and German immigrants since the 17th century, and "boer" is Afrikaans for "farmer." When the Boers were pioneering, spices and vinegar helped to preserve meat, so coriander seed became the main seasoning. South African law has strict rules for boerewors, for example the meat content must exceed 90 percent. It is the indispensable star of the braai and is also often sold in the street in hot-dog form.
